stemMd: Although the novelist's defenders describe the revisions she made for the second edition as ______, a comparison of the two texts shows that she cut three whole chapters and changed the fate of the heroine.
instructionsMd: Select exactly two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences alike in meaning. There is no credit for a partially correct selection.
explanationMd:
"Although" sets the defenders' description against what the comparison shows. So the blank must be the opposite of the evidence.

**Step 1 — the evidence.** She cut three whole chapters and changed the heroine's fate. Those are deep, structural changes.

**Step 2 — reverse it.** The defenders must describe the revisions as the opposite: slight, surface-level, touching only the appearance of the text.

**Step 3 — the pair.** **"Cosmetic"** (affecting only the surface) and **"superficial"** (not going below the surface) both produce the sentence *the defenders call the changes minor, but they were major.* **The answer is cosmetic and superficial.**

**How to check.** Read the completed sentence and make sure "although" introduces a real contrast. With the pair of words meaning *wide-ranging*, the defenders and the comparison agree and "although" has nothing to concede. With "judicious", the sentence is grammatical and even plausible (defenders often call revisions wise), but a wise revision can cut three chapters, so there is no contrast, and in any case no other choice means *judicious*.

distractorRationale.e: "Sweeping" means wide-ranging. It pairs with "extensive", but a sweeping revision is exactly what the comparison reveals, so the defenders' description would agree with the evidence and the "although" would have nothing to set against it.
distractorRationale.c: "Extensive" is the other half of the wide-ranging pair and fails in the same way: it makes the defenders' description match the evidence rather than contrast with it.
distractorRationale.b: "Judicious" means wise and well judged. It is what defenders might well say, but wisdom is compatible with cutting whole chapters, so it creates no contrast with the evidence, and it has no partner among the choices.
distractorRationale.f: "Belated" means coming late. The evidence concerns how much was changed, not when, so it sets up no contrast, and no other choice shares its meaning.

accessibilityText: A sentence with one blank. Although the novelist's defenders describe the revisions she made for the second edition as blank, a comparison of the two texts shows that she cut three whole chapters and changed the fate of the heroine. The six choices are superficial, judicious, extensive, cosmetic, sweeping and belated. Select exactly two choices that fit the sentence and produce completed sentences alike in meaning. There is no credit for a partially correct selection.

provenance.notes: Original Sentence Equivalence item written for wave 7. The novelist and her editions are invented. The decoy pair sweeping and extensive is alike in meaning but cancels the concessive contrast; judicious fits the sentence grammatically and plausibly but has no partner and creates no contrast. Not adapted from any ETS item.

independentSolve.workingNotes: 'Although' sets up a contrast with the major changes (three chapters cut, the heroine's fate changed), so the defenders must call the revisions minor: superficial or cosmetic. Extensive and sweeping are a pair, but they agree with the evidence instead of contrasting with it. Judicious and belated have no partner. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave7-gre-verbal-run1) reached the same answer: 'Although' sets the defenders' description against major changes (three chapters cut, the heroine's fate changed), so the defenders must have called the revisions minor: superficial and cosmetic. Extensive and sweeping describe what the comparison shows, not the defenders' description. Judicious and belated have no partners and do not create the needed contrast.]

review.notes: Author solved as cosmetic and superficial, twice.
